neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 14 (E4V4M6). Mildly confused, oriented to person and place but not to date (off by 3 weeks). Speech is slow but fluent. Concentration mildly impaired. Registration 3/3, recall 1/3 at five minutes. No aphasia or dysarthria.

Visual fields full to confrontation. Bilateral papilledema (grade II) on fundoscopic exam. Facial sensation intact. Facial strength symmetric. Hearing intact bilaterally. Oral thrush present on palate and buccal mucosa. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.motor: Strength 5/5 in all extremities. Mildly reduced muscle bulk diffusely — generalized wasting. Normal tone.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception in all extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in bilateral upper and lower extremities. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.

neurological_exam.additional: Notably absent meningismus — no neck stiffness, Kernig sign negative, Brudzinski sign negative. This is a critical finding: meningismus is often absent in cryptococcal meningitis due to the organism's polysaccharide capsule causing less meningeal inflammation. Visual obscurations reported by patient — transient bilateral visual graying lasting seconds, occurring several times per hour, suggestive of raised intracranial pressure. Generalized wasting with temporal muscle wasting bilaterally. Weight loss of approximately 10 kg over 3 months per patient report.

patient.chief_complaint: Worst headache of my life getting worse over 3 weeks
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darius Washington is a 48-year-old right-handed African American man who presents to the emergency department with a 4-week history of progressive headache that he describes as 'the worst headache of my life.' The headache began approximately 4 weeks ago as a dull, generalized pressure sensation that he initially attributed to work stress. Over the first two weeks, it gradually intensified and became constant. He tried over-the-counter ibuprofen and acetaminophen with minimal relief. Over the past two weeks, the headache has become severe, particularly in the morning upon waking, and is now accompanied by nausea (no vomiting), blurred vision, and a sense of cognitive slowing. He reports transient episodes of bilateral visual graying lasting several seconds, occurring multiple times per hour for the past 5 days — these visual obscurations are concerning for raised intracranial pressure. He has lost approximately 10 kg over the past 3 months without intentional dieting. He reports night sweats for the past 6 weeks. He was seen by his dentist 2 weeks ago for a routine cleaning, at which time oral thrush was noted and he was prescribed nystatin. He has not seen a doctor in approximately 8 years and has no known medical history. He recently separated from his long-term male partner of 15 years and is currently living alone. He denies any history of HIV testing. He denies intravenous drug use but acknowledges prior recreational cocaine use in his 20s-30s. He denies recent travel, tick exposure, or known sick contacts. He reports decreased appetite and fatigue for the past 2 months. Importantly, he describes the headache as 'gradually building' rather than sudden or thunderclap in onset, which helps distinguish this from subarachnoid hemorrhage despite his description of it being the 'worst headache.'

mri.impression: Communicating hydrocephalus with mild ventriculomegaly (Evans index 0.32). Multiple non-enhancing cystic foci in bilateral basal ganglia (caudate heads and lentiform nuclei) following CSF signal on all sequences, consistent with dilated/gelatinous perivascular spaces. No leptomeningeal enhancement; note that absent enhancement does not exclude meningeal infection in a severely immunocompromised host. No acute infarcts. Pattern carries an infectious/inflammatory differential (see below); CSF analysis required for characterisation. Clinical correlation recommended.

differential_by_imaging.rationale: Bilateral basal ganglia non-enhancing cystic/gelatinous perivascular spaces, combined with communicating hydrocephalus and absent leptomeningeal enhancement in an immunocompromised patient, are a recognised MRI pattern of CNS cryptococcosis; CSF microbiology and antigen testing required to characterise

Ventriculomegaly with periventricular signal change could superficially suggest NPH; however, the basal ganglia cystic foci and the markedly elevated opening pressure (38 cmH2O) on this study are atypical for NPH

CNS lymphoma in HIV/AIDS typically presents as ring-enhancing or homogeneously enhancing mass lesions with surrounding edema; the absence of any enhancing mass lesion on this study makes lymphoma less likely

optimal_actions.action: Obtain non-contrast CT head to exclude mass effect, midline shift, basal cistern obliteration, or hydrocephalus that would contraindicate lumbar puncture in this patient with altered mental status and/or immunocompromise.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Absence of mass lesion, midline shift, or signs of impending herniation — confirms LP is safe.

optimal_actions.action: Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures BEFORE the first antibiotic dose and send CBC with differential, CMP, procalcitonin, CRP, and lactate.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Peripheral leukocytosis with left shift, elevated procalcitonin/CRP, eventual blood-culture growth of the pathogen.

optimal_actions.action: Verify compatibility and interactions of induction antifungal therapy (liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine) with the patient's antiretroviral regimen and existing medications.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No prohibitive interactions; confirmation of standard guideline-directed empiric regimen with dose adjustments as required.

optimal_actions.action: Search the literature for current guideline-directed empiric antibiotic selection by age and host factors and for the evidence base supporting adjunctive dexamethasone in pneumococcal meningitis.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Retrieval of IDSA 2004, ESCMID 2016, and De Gans 2002 to support empiric regimen and steroid timing.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain contrast-enhanced brain MRI to assess for parenchymal complications (cerebritis, abscess, subdural empyema, ventriculitis, venous sinus thrombosis, infarction).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Leptomeningeal enhancement; identification or exclusion of complications that modify management.

useless_tools.rationale: No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

harmful_tools.rationale: Imaging in this case demonstrates space-occupying lesions and/or significant hydrocephalus with elevated intracranial pressure; performing lumbar puncture in this setting risks cerebral herniation. CSF sampling should only follow neurosurgical consultation and ICP-lowering measures.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture whenever any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal neurological deficit, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60). LP performed in undetected mass effect can precipitate fatal herniation.

Blood cultures must be drawn (under interpret_labs) before the first dose of empiric antibiotics so that culture yield is not lost; in practice this means peripheral cultures are collected at the same draw as the CSF analysis is initiated, and the lab tube sequencing prevents antibiotic exposure before specimen acquisition.

critical_actions: Initiate induction antifungal therapy with liposomal amphotericin B (3-4 mg/kg/day IV) plus flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day PO divided q6h) for at least 2 weeks.
Manage elevated intracranial pressure aggressively with serial therapeutic lumbar punctures targeting opening pressure <20 cmH2O; consider lumbar drain if refractory.
Confirm HIV status, obtain CD4 count and viral load, and coordinate ART initiation (typically delayed 4-6 weeks after antifungal start to mitigate IRIS).
Send CSF cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) titre and fungal culture; obtain serum CrAg.
Screen for and treat concurrent opportunistic infections.
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT proceed to lumbar puncture: imaging shows mass effect / significant hydrocephalus and LP risks cerebral herniation until ICP is managed and neurosurgery has cleared the procedure.
Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
Do NOT initiate antiretroviral therapy concurrently with antifungal induction; delay ART 4-6 weeks to reduce IRIS risk.
Do NOT use fluconazole monotherapy for induction in CNS cryptococcosis.
key_reasoning_points: Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis presents with high opening pressure and a relatively bland CSF cell count; opening pressure must be measured at every LP.
Multiple basal-ganglia 'pseudocysts' following CSF signal on MRI is a classic imaging pattern of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis.
India ink, serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen, and fungal culture are the diagnostic tests; culture is the gold standard.
Induction therapy with liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine is non-negotiable in CNS disease.
Therapeutic LP is the first-line intervention for elevated ICP; refractory cases require lumbar drain or VP shunt.
ART timing matters: starting ART too early risks IRIS — delay 4-6 weeks after antifungal start.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Lower the index of suspicion for bacterial meningitis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Gram-stain sensitivity is only 60-90% even untreated; multiplex PCR and antigen testing must be used to confirm the organism.

metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Chronic meningitis in a patient with undiagnosed HIV/AIDS. Absent meningismus, minimal fever, clear CSF, and only mild pleocytosis may mislead the clinician. Markedly elevated ICP is the critical finding requiring urgent management.
clinical_pearls: Elevated ICP management (serial therapeutic LPs) is the single most important intervention in cryptococcal meningitis survival
CSF cryptococcal antigen has >95% sensitivity and >95% specificity — it is the gold standard rapid diagnostic test
ART initiation must be delayed 4-6 weeks in CNS cryptococcosis to prevent fatal IRIS (COAT trial, NEJM 2014)
Corticosteroids are harmful in cryptococcal meningitis — unlike TB meningitis where dexamethasone saves lives
Gelatinous pseudocysts in basal ganglia are pathognomonic MRI findings for CNS cryptococcosis
